A *tune-up* fixed the rough idle.

gloss: The adjustment of the wheels so the car runs straight.
examples: The pothole ruined my *wheel alignment*.
*Wheel alignments* are cheap compared to new tires.
Get a *wheel alignment* if the car pulls to one side.

gloss: A check of how much pollution a vehicle's exhaust produces.
examples: The car failed its *emissions test*.
Some states require *emissions tests* every two years.
You can't renew the tags without an *emissions test*.

gloss: A place or machine that cleans vehicles.
examples: Run it through the *car wash* on the way home.
Two new *car washes* opened on that road.
The *car wash* broke my antenna.

gloss: A garage that repairs damaged car bodies and paint.
examples: The *body shop* said it would take a week.
Insurance keeps a list of approved *body shops*.
My car is still at the *body shop*.

gloss: A yard full of wrecked cars where used parts are sold.
examples: He found a door at the *junkyard* for thirty bucks.
*Junkyards* out here stretch for acres.
The old truck finally went to the *junkyard*.
contrast: Americans say junkyard; the British say scrapyard.

gloss: A business licensed to sell cars of a particular make.
examples: We bought it from a *dealership* across town.
Three *dealerships* sit side by side on that road.
The *dealership* handles the paperwork for you.

gloss: A short drive taken to see whether you want to buy a car.
examples: Take it for a *test drive* before you decide.
We did three *test drives* in one afternoon.
The *test drive* sold him on the car.

gloss: A car that has had an earlier owner.
examples: Her first *used car* cost two thousand dollars.
*Used cars* got expensive after the shortage.
Have a mechanic look at any *used car* first.
contrast: Here used ends in a z sound, /juːzd/; in used to it is /juːst/, with an s.

gloss: An old car given to a dealer as part of the payment for a new one.
examples: They gave me four thousand for my *trade-in*.
The lot was full of *trade-ins*.
Your *trade-in* has to be paid off first.

gloss: The mirror on the outside of a car door.
examples: A truck clipped my *side mirror*.
Fold the *side mirrors* in before the car wash.
Adjust the *side mirror* before you pull out.
contrast: Americans say side mirror; the British say wing mirror.

gloss: The red light at the back of a car that comes on when the driver brakes.
examples: Your left *brake light* is out.
A wall of *brake lights* appeared ahead of us.
The *brake light* costs a few dollars to replace.
contrast: Brake sounds exactly like break but is spelled with a-k-e.

gloss: The blinking lights a driver turns on to warn others of trouble.
examples: Put your *hazard lights* on if you stop on the shoulder.
His *hazard lights* were flashing in the breakdown lane.
She left the *hazard lights* going while she changed the tire.
contrast: Used only in the plural; also called flashers in everyday speech.

gloss: The brightest setting of a car's headlights, for empty dark roads.
examples: Turn off your *high beams* when a car comes toward you.
The *high beams* lit up the whole field.
He flashed his *high beams* to warn us.
contrast: Used only in the plural; the British say full beam or main beam.

gloss: The dial showing how much fuel is left in the tank.
examples: The *fuel gauge* has been stuck on full for a week.
Old *fuel gauges* are not very accurate.
Keep an eye on the *fuel gauge* out here.
contrast: Gauge is pronounced GAYJ despite the spelling.

gloss: The warning lamp on the dashboard that says the engine needs attention.
examples: The *check engine light* came on again this morning.
*Check engine lights* can mean almost anything.
He drove for months with the *check engine light* on.

gloss: The system that holds a car at a set speed without the driver pressing the pedal.
examples: I set the *cruise control* at seventy.
Don't use *cruise control* on icy roads.
The rental car has *cruise control* and a backup camera.

gloss: The small remote that locks, unlocks and often starts a car.
examples: The battery in my *key fob* died.
Both *key fobs* came with the car.
Press the *key fob* twice to unlock all the doors.

gloss: A small camera mounted on the windshield that records the road.
examples: The *dash cam* caught the whole thing.
*Dash cams* have gotten cheap.
Insurance asked for the *dash cam* footage.

gloss: A printed map showing the roads of an area.
examples: There's an old *road map* in the glove compartment.
Gas stations used to give away *road maps*.
He unfolded the *road map* across the hood.

gloss: The flap above the windshield that a driver folds down against the sun.
examples: Flip the *sun visor* down, the glare is awful.
Both *sun visors* have little mirrors.
The parking pass clips to the *sun visor*.

gloss: The system that clears ice or fog from a car's windows.
examples: Turn on the *defroster* before you pull out.
The rear *defroster* stopped working.
Old cars had weak *defrosters*.
contrast: Americans say defroster; the British say demister.

gloss: The safety seat that straps a small child into a vehicle.
examples: The baby screamed the whole way in the *car seat*.
We had two *car seats* across the back.
The hospital won't let you leave without a *car seat*.
contrast: In American usage a car seat is almost always the child's safety seat, not just any seat in a car.

gloss: A raised seat that lifts an older child so the seat belt fits properly.
examples: She's big enough for a *booster seat* now.
We keep two *booster seats* in the van.
Kids ride in a *booster seat* until they're about eight.

gloss: The seat behind the driver and front passenger.
examples: Throw your bag in the *back seat*.
The *back seats* fold down for cargo.
The kids fought in the *back seat* the whole way.

gloss: The front seat next to the driver.
examples: My coffee is in the cup holder by the *passenger seat*.
Both *passenger seats* were full of groceries.
He rode in the *passenger seat* and navigated.

gloss: A sticker with a slogan that a driver puts on the back of a car.
examples: Her car is covered in *bumper stickers*.
The *bumper sticker* made me laugh at the red light.
He peeled the old *bumper sticker* off before selling it.
